title: Lunar dust shields move from lab benches to field trials
paragraphs: Moon dust is fine, sharp and surprisingly sticky.
It clings to suits, lenses and solar panels, and it can wear down moving parts within days.
Engineers want equipment that is resilient enough to keep working after long exposure to it.
One approach uses a thin film of electrodes that pushes charged grains away from a surface.
In early lab tests, the film cleared most of the dust from a glass panel in under a minute.
The team then had to adapt the design for vacuum chambers that mimic conditions on the Moon.
They gradually increased the amount of dust and the length of each test.
Field trials will take into account temperature swings, uneven ground and the limited power a lander can allocate to cleaning.
If the shields stay consistent over months, they could sustain longer missions.
In the long run, the same idea may help keep solar farms on Earth cleaner as well.

title: Quieter supersonic flight moves closer to community tests
paragraphs: Engineers are preparing an experimental jet to fly over several towns and record how people hear its softer sonic thump.
Older supersonic planes produced a loud boom that rattled windows, so flights over land were restricted.
The new aircraft has a long, narrow nose and carefully shaped wings that spread out the pressure waves.
Instead of one sharp boom, people on the ground should hear something closer to a distant car door.
Volunteers in each town will be asked to describe what they heard and whether it bothered them.
Microphones placed along the flight path will capture the sound at the same time.
Researchers will compare the recordings with the survey answers to see how well their models predict real reactions.
The results could help regulators decide whether quieter supersonic flights should be allowed over land.
If so, a trip across the country might one day take only a few hours.

title: Trade cards: tiny advertisements from the 1880s
author: Dana Whitfield
paragraphs: Long before glossy magazines, shopkeepers handed out small printed cards to remind customers of their names and wares.
These trade cards were cheap to produce and easy to keep.
Many people collected them in albums, so a number of them survive today.
The cards often showed bright pictures that had little to do with the product.
A card for a hardware store might feature a kitten, a ship or a famous building.
On the back, the merchant printed an address, a list of goods and sometimes a short poem.
Historians use the cards to study how small businesses tried to stand out in crowded towns.
They also reveal which products were new, from sewing machines to canned food.
Looking at a full album, you can watch advertising slowly learn to sell a feeling as well as a thing.
The collection is open to researchers, and many of the cards can be viewed online.
